newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan wary of China in drafting U.S. defence pact.
newsitem.headline: Japan wary of China in drafting U.S. defence pact.

text.p: Japan and the United States are set to announce an interim report next month on a review of their 20-year-old old defence cooperation agreement, but Tokyo is trying hard to limit the scope of the new pact.
The reason is China -- and Japan's own pacifist constitution.
Beijing has time and again warned Tokyo that a U.S.-Japan military alliance reshaped for the post-Cold War era should not target China.
And Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and other Japanese leaders have gone out of their way to publicly assure China that no such thing will happen.
"We promise to be fully transparent (to the world) with the (new) guideline on defence cooperation," Hashimoto said last month in Washington after meeting with President Bill Clinton.
"And new measures will be within the bounds of the (Japanese) constitution," he added.
The next day China's official People's Daily ran a column urging Hashimoto to keep his word, using an old Chinese proverb that "one must do what he says and do it with earnest".
The review of the 1978 "Guideline" of U.S.-Japan Defence Cooperation was announced during Clinton's visit to Tokyo in April 1996 and started last November.
The final document is to be revealed in November this year.

The 1978 document listed contingency plans for a Soviet invasion of Japan, but did not include any other possible scenario, such as a conflict on the Korean Peninsula, or over the Taiwan Strait or the disputed Spratly Islands.
A clause in the 1978 document said the agreement does not require either government to enact new laws or allot new budgets, a clause designed to silence Japan's leftist opposition at the time.
When the review began last year, Japan agreed to include discussions over a possible Korean Peninsula conflict, but refused to discuss Taiwan or the Spratlys, government sources said.

Japan did agree to scrap the "no budget, no law" clause, in effect promising that the new guideline will be backed by specific legal measures involving almost all branches of government besides the Defence Ministry.
But Japan has refused a NATO-like cooperation agreement -- Washington has always wanted a watered-down version with Tokyo -- because of its 1947 pacifist constitution.
Article 9 of the U.S.-drafted constitution bars Japan from using military means to settle any international dispute.
Successive Japanese governments have maintained that the same article bans Japan from entering into "collective security" or offensive military alliances.
Hashimoto, known as a hawk who wanted amendment of the no-war clause while just in the ranks of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), has sidestepped the issues since becoming prime minister.
He was named premier in January 1995 on the strength of his party's parliamentary alliance with the pacifist Socialists, who have stubbornly defended Article 9.

The Socialists remain as Hashimoto's unlikely allies in parliament, although Japanese politics is rife with speculation that he might soon abandon the tiny Socialists and form a "grand alliance" with the conservative main opposition party, Shinshinto (New Frontier Party).
Hashimoto's pledge on the constitution means Japanese cooperation with the United States in a conflict on the Korean Peninsula would be limited to non-combat support behind the front lines.
It would include medical treatment of U.S. troops in Japan, providing airport facilities and clearing minefields.

But much cooperation is locked in an unclear "grey zone" between outright offensive cooperation and defensive help, for example over the question of Japanese navy minesweepers operating in international waters.
"I would not count on next month's interim report to spell out all of these grey zone issues," one government official said.
